readings.c1s2:
¶
'''wrasse''' (ras), ''n.'' [Also, better, ''wrass''; said to be < W. ''gwrachen'', the W. name for the fish being ''gwrachen y môr''.] An acanthopterygian teleost fish of the family ''Labridæ''; any labrid, or labroid fish, having thick fleshy lips, strong sharp teeth, and usually brilliant coloration. See ''parrot-fish'' (with cut). {{smaller|They are carnivorous salt-water fishes of littoral habits, haunting chiefly rocky shores, and many of them are esteemed food-fishes. The species to which the name applies as a book-name are very numerous; but those of which ''wrasse'' is actually spoken are chiefly the British species, as the ballan-wrasse and the red wrasse. (See cut under ''Labrus''.) In America the best-known wrasses (though not so called) are the common cunner, the tautog, and the fathead. See cuts under these words.—'''Comber wrasse.''' Same as ''comber''<sup>3</sup>, 2.—'''Cook wrasse,''' the striped wrasse, ''Labrus mixtus''.—'''Ctenoid wrasses,''' wrasses with ctenoid scales; the ''Ctenolabridæ''.—'''Cycloid wrasses,''' wrasses with cycloid scales; the ''Cyclolabridæ''.—'''Servellan wrasse.''' Same as ''sweetlips'', 3.—'''Small-mouthed wrasse,''' ''Centrolabrus exoletus''. (See also ''ballan-wrasse, rainbow-wrasse''.)}}

'''wrasse-fish''' (ras′fish), ''n.'' A wrasse. See ''Labrus'' (with cut).

'''wrastle''' (ras′l), ''v.'' and ''n.'' An obsolete or dialectal form of ''wrestle''.

'''wrath''' (räth, sometimes râth), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wraththe, wratthe, wræththe, wreththe, wrathe, wrethe'', also erroneously ''wraugth'', < AS. (ONorth.) ''wrǣththo, wrǣtho'' (= Icel. ''reithi'' (for *''vreithi'') = Sw. Dan. ''vrede''), anger, wrath, < ''wrāth'', angry, wroth: see ''wroth''. ''Wrath'' is thus the noun of ''wroth''. The historical pron. is räth, which is also almost or quite universal in the United States.] '''1.''' Fierce anger; vehement indignation; rage.
readings.c1s4: wrath or anger in; anger; enrage.

readings.c3s2:
{{smaller block|No Roman fleet came to ''wreak'' the Imperial revenge on the German shore. {{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Amer. Lects., p. 121.}}}}

¶
'''wreak<sup>1</sup>†''' (rēk), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wreke'', ''wrake'', ''wreche'' (= D. ''wraak''); < ''wreak''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' Revenge; vengeance; furious passion; resentment.
{{smaller block|For syn thou take no ''wreke'' on me.
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 105.}}
<poem>I drede of thyn unhappe,
Lest for thy gilt the ''wreche'' of Love procede
On alle hem that ben hore and rounde of shape,
That ben so lykly folk in love to spede.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Envoy of Chaucer to Scogan, l. 30.}}
<poem>Our writings are,
By any envious instruments that dare
Apply them to the guilty, made to speak
What they will have to fit their tyrannous ''wreak''.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sejanus, iv. 3.}}
<poem>If revenge
And unexpected ''wreak'' were ever pleasing,
Or could endear the giver of such blessings,
All these I come adorn’d with.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, iv. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Punishment.
{{smaller block|<poem>Therto we wreched wommen nothyne konne,
When us is wo, but sitte and wepe and thynke;
Our ''wreche'' is this oure owen wo to drynke.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 784.}}}}

'''wreak<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v.'' An erroneous spelling of ''reck''.

'''wreaker''' (rē′kėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wreker'', ''wrekeer'' (= MD. ''wreker''), avenger; < ''wreak''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who wreaks.
{{smaller block|The stork, the ''wrekere'' of avouterye.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 361.}}
<poem>Infernal Furies eke, ye ''wreakers'' of wrong, . . .
Receive these words, and eke your heavy power
Withdraw from me.</poem>
{{right|''Surrey'', Æneid, iv.}}}}
readings.c3s3:
{{smaller block|If we let sin alone, his kingdom flourisheth; if we strike at him, and hit not the bough he sits on, we move him not; if we do, we are judged partial, personal, and ''wreakers'' of our own spleen. {{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 465.}}}}

¶
'''wreakful†''' (rēk′fu̇l), ''a.'' [Also ''wreckful''; < ME. ''wrakeful''; < ''wreak'' + ''-ful''.] Revengeful; angry.
{{smaller block|<poem>What thing is love? It is a power divine,
That reigns in us, or else a ''wreakful'' law.</poem>
{{right|''Greene'', Sonnetto.}}
Working ''wreakefull'' vengeance on my Foes.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., v. 2. 32 (fol. 1623).}}}}

'''wreakless<sup>1</sup>†''' (rēk′les), ''a.'' [< ''wreak''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less''.] Unpunished; unavenged.
{{smaller block|<poem>You still ''wreakless'' live,
Gnaw, vermin-like, things sacred, no laws give
To your devouring.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Odyssey, ii. 223.}}}}

'''wreakless<sup>2</sup>†''', ''a.'' An erroneous spelling of ''reckless''.

'''wreath''' (rēth), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wrethe'', ''wræthe'', < AS. ''wrǣth'', a twisted band, bandage, < ''writhan'' (pret. ''wrāth''), writhe, twist: see ''writhe''.] '''1.''' A twisted band; something twisted, as a flowering branch, into a circular form; especially, a sort of crown made of natural or artificial flowers sewed to a stem, or of thin metal-work, filigree, or the like; a garland; a chaplet.
{{smaller block|<poem>A ''wrethe'' of gold arm-greet, of huge wighte,
Upon his heed, set ful of stones brighte.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 1287.}}}}

The historical pron. is räth, which is also almost or quite universal in the United States.]   '''1.''' Fierce anger; vehement indignation; rage. {{smaller block|Yet in his ''wraugth'' this thought he euer among: If he shuld avenge hym sodenly, All his pepill wold say he did hym wrong. {{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1373.}}}} {{smaller block|''Wraththe'' of children is ouercome soone. {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 31.}}}} {{smaller block|Then boyling ''Wrath'', stern, cruell, swift, and rash, That like a Boar her teeth doth grinde and gnash. {{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Furies.}}}} '''2†.''' Heat; impetuosity. {{smaller block|They are in the very ''wrath'' of love, and they will together; clubs cannot part them. {{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, v. 2. 44.}}}} '''3.''' The effects of anger; the just punishment of an offense or crime; vengeance. Rom. xiii. 4. —'''To pour out vials of wrath.''' {{smaller|See ''vial''. ='''Syn. 1.''' ''Anger'', ''Vexation'', ''Indignation'', etc. (see ''anger''1).}} '''wrath†''' (räth), ''a.'' An obsolete (in early modern use erroneous) form of ''wroth''. {{smaller block|Whereat the Prince full ''wrath'' his strong right hand In full avengement heaved up on hie. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. viii. 43.}}}} {{smaller block|Oberon is passing fell and ''wrath''. {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., ii. 1. 20.}}}} '''wrath†''' (räth), ''v.''   [< ME. ''wraththen'', ''wratthen'', ''wrathen'', ''wrathien'', < AS. ''gewrāthian'' (= OS. ''wrēthian'' = Icel. ''reitha''), be angry, < ''wrāth'', angry: see ''wroth'' and ''wrath'', ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To become wroth or angry; manifest anger. {{smaller block|Than the worthy at his wife ''wrathet'' a little, And blamyt the burde for hir bold speche. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 8442.}}}} {{smaller block|And appere in hus presence whyle hym pleye lyketh, And yf he ''wratthe'', we mowe be war and hus way roume. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), i. 189.}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make wroth or angry; cause wrath or anger in; anger; enrage. {{smaller block|him, and with his owne propre Swerd he was slayn. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 37.}}}} {{smaller block|I wol not ''wrathe'' him, also mote I thryve. {{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Manciple’s Tale, l. 80.}}}} {{smaller block|And that es drede perfite in vs and gastely when we drede to ''wrethe'' God in the leste syne that we kane knawe and flese it als venyme. {{right|''Hampole'', Prose Treatises (E. E. T. S.), p. 12.}}}} '''2.''' To be angry with; exhibit anger or wrath to. {{smaller block|Whi ''wraththist'' thou me? y greue thee nouȝt. Whi art thou to thi freend vnkinde? {{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 161.}}}} '''wrathful''' (räth′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wrethful'', ''wrethvol'', wrathful; < ''wrath'', ''n.'', + ''-ful''.]   '''1.''' Full of wrath; very angry; greatly incensed. {{smaller block|Strong men, and ''wrathful'' that a stranger knight Should do and almost overdo the deeds Of Lancelot. {{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}} '''2.''' Expressive of or prompted or characterized by wrath or anger; raging; impetuous; furious: as, ''wrathful'' passions; a ''wrathful'' countenance. {{smaller block|How now, lords! your ''wrathful'' weapons drawn Here in our presence? {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2. 237.}}}} {{smaller block|Like Lightning, swift the ''wrathful'' Faulchion flew. {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, x. 524.}}}} '''3.''' Executing wrath; serving as the instrument of wrath. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Whiles we, God’s ''wrathful'' agent, do correct Their proud contempt that beats His peace to heaven. {{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 87.}}}} ='''Syn. 1.''' {{smaller|Indignant, resentful, exasperated, irate.}} '''wrathfully''' (räth′fu̇l-i), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''wrethfully''; < ''wrathful'' + ''-ly''2.]   In a wrathful manner; with anger; angrily. {{smaller block|Then thes Paynymes ''wrethfully'' ther thens
Whent, leuying anon ther stourdy uiolens. {{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2218.}}}} {{smaller block|Kill him boldly, but not ''wrathfully.'' {{right|''Shak.'', J. C., ii. 1. 172.}}}} '''wrathfulness''' (räth′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being wrathful; vehement anger. '''wrathily''' (rä′thi-li), ''adv.''   [< ''wrathy'' + ''-ly''2.]   With wrath or great anger; angrily. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|The master ''wrathily'' insisted. {{right|''G. W. Cable'', Old Creole Days, Posson Jone.}}}} '''wrathless''' (räth′les), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wraththelees''; < ''wrath'', ''n.'', + ''-less''.]   Free from anger.   ''Waller'', Of the Countess of Carlisle’s Chamber. '''wrathy''' (rä′thi), ''a.''   [< ''wrath'', ''n.'', + ''-y''1.]   Angry. [Colloq.] '''wraw†''', ''a.''   [ME. ''wraw'', ''wrah'', ''wroȝ'', pl. ''wrowe'', perverse, angry, fierce; cf. ''wro'', a corner.]   Angry; froward; peevish. {{smaller block|With this speche the cook wex wroth and ''wraw.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Manciple’s Tale, l. 46.}}}} '''wrawful†''', ''a.''   [ME., < ''wraw'' + ''-ful''.]   Peevish; angry. {{smaller block|Ire troubleth a man, and accidie maketh hym hevy, thoghtful, and ''wrawful.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}}} '''wrawl†''', ''v. i.''   [Prob. a var. of ''wawl'', ''waul''.]   To cry as a cat; waul; whine; moan. Nor practize snuffingly to speake, for that doth imitate The brutish Storke and Elephant, yea, and the ''wralling'' cat. {{smaller block|{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 293.}}}} {{smaller block|Cats that ''wrawling'' still did cry. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. xii. 27.}}}} '''wrawness†''', ''n.''   [< ME. ''wrawnesse'', perverseness, peevishness; < ''wraw'' + ''-ness''.]   Anger; peevishness; frowardness. {{smaller block|He dooth alle thyng with anoy, and with ''wrawnesse'', slaknesse, and excusacioun. {{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}}} '''wraxling''' (raks′ling), ''a.''
